# Marcus

Marcus sits in the waiting room with his hands folded in his lap, the posture of someone accustomed to discipline and order. At sixty-seven, his military bearing is still evident—shoulders squared, jaw set—though his eyes carry a weariness that suggests the body's rigidity masks something far more fragile.

Eighteen months ago, Marcus was driving home from the VA hospital where he volunteers as a peer counselor. He'd spent thirty-two years as a combat medic, and retirement hadn't diminished his need to be useful. The accident happened on a clear afternoon on a familiar stretch of highway. A delivery truck crossed the center line without warning. Marcus remembers the sound—a screech of tires, then the violent crunch of metal. His car spun twice before hitting the guardrail. He was trapped for forty minutes before emergency services extracted him.

He sustained a fractured collarbone, three broken ribs, and a concussion. The physical injuries have largely healed, but Marcus describes the accident as if it happened yesterday. He replays the moment the truck appeared, frame by frame, analyzing what he might have done differently. Could he have swerved sooner? Should he have been driving slower? His medic's training kicks in unbidden—he finds himself assessing the angles of impact, calculating force vectors, wondering if he would have survived had he been sitting three inches to the left.

Since the collision, Marcus avoids driving. His daughter handles the errands now, and he's given up his volunteer work at the hospital. The irony isn't lost on him. For three decades, he'd trained himself to remain calm under catastrophic circumstances. He'd held dying soldiers' hands, made split-second decisions about triage, compartmentalized horror into clinical action. But now, sitting in the passenger seat while his daughter navigates traffic, his chest tightens. His palms sweat. He finds himself bracing against the door frame at every intersection, his body anticipating collision.

At night, Marcus lies awake. When he does sleep, he dreams of the accident—except in the dreams, he's unable to move. His legs won't respond. He's back in the car, watching the truck approach, powerless. He wakes gasping, his heart hammering, and he lies in the dark for hours, afraid to close his eyes again. His wife, Eleanor, used to anchor him through these moments. She'd hold his hand and remind him he was safe. Eleanor died four years ago from cancer, and Marcus has lived alone since. He's learned to sit with the nightmares without her steadying presence.

What troubles Marcus most is the loss of identity. He's always been the person who responds, who fixes things, who remains steady when others fall apart. Now he's hypervigilant in ways he can't control. When his daughter's car hits a pothole, adrenaline floods his system. He snaps at her over minor things—the speed she's driving, the distance she maintains from other vehicles—and then feels crushing guilt. He knows his behavior is irrational. He knows this intellectually in the way only someone trained in emergency medicine can know it. But knowledge doesn't quiet the alarm bells his nervous system has installed.

He's withdrawn from his friends, declined invitations, stopped attending his book club. The world feels unpredictable now in a way it didn't before, even after decades in combat zones. A combat medic trains for danger; he expects it, prepares for it, controls what variables he can. But an ordinary afternoon on an ordinary highway? That randomness terrifies him in a way he can't quite articulate.

Marcus is here because his daughter insisted, and because part of him—the part that still remembers how to ask for help—knows he can't continue like this. He's not sure what healing looks like when you've spent your entire life being the healer.
